darbha
(‘that which cuts asunder’)
------------------------------------------
Right from the Vedic times certain varieties of grass like the दर्भ have been considered as sacred and have been used in the sacrificial rites. Since a dry piece of this grass can cut our skin (dṛ = to cut) it might have got this name. Sometimes it has been identified with the कुश grass and sometimes described as different. But in today’s ritualistic practices the two names refer to the same (kuśa) grass.
In the Atharvaveda (6.43) it is mentioned that it can be used as an amulet for protection against certain evils.
Works on the आयुर्वेद predicate several uses to this grass such as appetising, purification of blood and semen, curing of certain diseases like jaundice and herpes.
The botanical names given for this grass are: Saccharum cylindricum or Poa cynosuroides.
See also KUŚA.

dārujaliṅga
(‘Śivaliṅga made out of wood’)
------------------------------------------
Unlike the other deities, शिव (one of the three aspects of the Supreme, the aspect of involution or withdrawal or destruction of the world) is invariably worshipped in the form of a लिङ्ग. A लिङ्ग is an icon, cylindrical in shape, with a spherical top. Since God is beyond name and form and since we cannot conceive of an abstract principle like him without the aid of concrete symbols, a spherical surface or emblem is perhaps the nearest approach to him.
‘Dāru’ means wood. Liṅgas carved out of wood are called ‘dārujaliṅgas’. They are of the sthāvara or stationary type. The minimum and maximum heights prescribed for such liṅgas are 16 and 144 aṅgulas. (One अङ्गुल is roughly 1.9 cms. or 0.75 inch.)
The dārujaliṅgas are classified into 9 or even 33 varieties, depending upon their height. For instance, if the मकर-लिङ्ग is 16 aṅgulas in height (the minimum height permitted), the daṇḍaliṅga is 80 aṅgulas and the phalodbhava लिङ्ग is 144 aṅgulas (the maximum permissible height).
As regards the type of wood out of which it is carved, about 20 varieties are recommended. Some of them are: शमी (Prosopsis spieigera), devadāru (Cedrus deodara), चन्दन (sandalwood), बिल्व (Aegle marmelos), अश्वत्थ (peepul tree) and अशोक (Saraca asoca).
See also LIṄGA.

darpaṇa
(‘[that] which increases one’s pride’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘darpaṇa’ is one of the common terms that indicates a mirror. It has been so called since it increases the ‘darpa’ or the pride of a beautiful or a handsome person!
A mirror is one of the several objects that is shown in the hands of a female figurine or a goddess, sculptured according to the rules of the मूर्तिशिल्पशास्त्र or Hindu इचोनोग्रफ्य्.
It is also one of the aṣṭamaṅgalas—eight objects signifying auspiciousness—normally used on auspicious occasions like the चोरोनतिओन् of a king.
See also AṢṬAMAṄGALAS.

Darśapūrṇamāsa
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices—called yajñas and yāgas—are an ancient institution. One of its varieties is ‘iṣṭi,’ a sacrifice performed with the four priests अध्वर्यु, आग्नीध्र, होतृ and ब्रह्मन्. (See under each title for details.) The दर्शपूर्णमास is a प्रकृति (an archetype) in this इष्टि group and is obligatory.
The words ‘darśa’ and ‘pūrṇamāsa’ actually stand for the new-मोओन् and the full-मोओन् days. Hence, the Vedic rites to be performed on these days have also been named ‘Darśa’ and ‘Pūrṇamāsa’. The two are identical in almost all respects except for some minor variations. Consequently, they are often clubbed together and called, ‘Darśapūrṇamāsa.’
The Darśa sacrifice is done on the new-मोओन् day and the day next to it (pratipad). The Pūrṇamāsa is performed on the full-मोओन् day and the following day.
The only difference in the procedure between these two sacrifices is that the पुरोडाश (rice-cake) is offered to इन्द्र and अग्नि in the Darśa whereas the same is offered to अग्नि-सोम in the Pūrṇamāsa.
The preliminaries like shaving, bathing and ड़स्तिन्ग् are done by the sacrificer on the day called ‘upavasaha’ (= ड़स्तिन्ग् and living near the fire). This is followed by anvādhāna (offering of three pieces of sacrificial wood into the fire). The other rites to follow are: पिण्डपितृयज्ञ (obsequial rites for the forefathers up to three generations); usual daily अग्निहोत्र; preparing the curdled milk for offering on the next day; preparing the पुरोडाश (rice-cakes) for offering; repetition of the सामिधेनी verses (eleven verses from the Ṛgveda, mostly from the third मण्डल, aimed at kindling the fire); āghāra libation (wherein the अध्वर्यु pours ghee into the fire moving the spoon all over, with appropriate mantras) and five प्रयाज and two ājyabhāga oblations (preliminary offerings).
Then, the principle offerings are made with पुरोडाश (rice-cakes) to the accompaniment of puro’nuvākyas (call or invitation to the deities by the होतृ priest) and yājyās (technical formulae of consecration chanted by the होतृ priest while the अध्वर्यु priest offers a libation of ghee).
In the Darśa, eleven offerings of पुरोडाश kept in small earthen plates are offered to इन्द्र and अग्नि. In the Pūrṇa-māsa, the offerings are made to अग्नि and सोम.
This is followed by the sviṣṭakṛt offering (a secondary offering to अग्नि by whose goodwill the sacrifice has been successfully done) and iḍābhakṣaṇa (eating the portions cut off from all the main offerings) by the priests.
Then comes अनुयाज (three supplementary offerings) followed by सूक्तवाक (speech of adoration by the होतृ priest) and śaṁyuvāka (formula of benediction, also by the होतृ priest).
After a few more minor rites like the patnīsaṁyāja (offerings to the consorts of the deities), removal of the योक्त्र (a belt of muñja grass), prāyaścittas (expiatory rites) and viṣṇukrama (ceremonially taking four steps with appropriate mantras, by the yajamāna or the sacrificer) the whole sacrifice comes to a close.
See also VEDIC SACRIFICES.

darśana
(‘seeing or experiencing’)
------------------------------------------
Though the word means ‘seeing’, it is often used in a technical sense, indicating any system of philosophy. Generally the Indian philosophical systems are called ‘darśanas’ since they claim to have been based on the ‘seeing’ or the ‘experiencing’ of the final truths.
These darśanas are classified into two broad groups: the आस्तिक-darśanas and the नास्तिक-darśanas. The former accept the authority of the वेदस् whereas the latter do not.
The former, being six in number, is often called ‘ṣaḍdarśanas’ (ṣaṭ = six) They are: the Nyāyadarśana of गौतम the Vaiśeṣikadarśana of कणाद the Sāṅkhyadarśana of कपिल the योगदर्शन of पतञ्जलि the Mīmāṁsādarśana of जैमिनि and the Vedāntadarśana of बादरायण. The latter are: the Cārvākadarśana of Cārvāka the Jainadarśana and the Bauddhadarśana.
The last two represent the various philosophical systems of जैनिस्म् and बुद्धिस्म्. The first represents मतेरिअलिस्म् of various shades and hues. Though the work itself is not available now, excerpts from it have been quoted in the treatises of other writers.
See under each title for details.
